content.definition: The inner nuclear layer consists of 8-12 rows of closely packed nuclei belonging to the bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, interplexiform cells and supportive Muller cells (Tripathi and Tripathi, 1984). Four layers can be distinguished by light microscopy (Fig 14.30): the outermost layer with horizontal cell nuclei; the outer intermediate layer with bipolar cell nuclei; the inner intermediate layer with Muller cell nuclei; and the innermost layer with amacrine and interplexiform cell nuclei. The layer houses the second-order neurons of the visual pathway (the bipolar and horizontal cells) together with the modulatory amacrine and interplexiform cells and the principal glia of the retina, the Muller cells.
content.location: The inner nuclear layer lies between the outer plexiform layer externally and the inner plexiform layer internally. The perikarya of the bipolar cells, approximately 9 um in diameter at the fovea and 5 um at the periphery of the retina (Sigelman and Ozanics, 1982), send their processes to both plexiform layers. The concentration of horizontal cells is highest at the fovea and decreases towards the periphery, although their processes branch more extensively towards the ora serrata; the somas of the amacrine cells lie internal to the nuclei of the Muller cells and are absent from the fovea; the nuclei of the interplexiform cells occupy the innermost part of the layer, and most of the inner intermediate layer is occupied by the cell bodies of the Muller cells, although their perikarya can be present in any sublayer (Figs 14.30 and 14.34).
layers: Outermost layer: the nuclei of the horizontal cells
Outer intermediate layer: the nuclei of the bipolar cells
Inner intermediate layer: the nuclei of the Muller cells, which occupy most of this sublayer although Muller perikarya may occur in any sublayer (Fig 14.34)
Innermost layer: the nuclei of the amacrine and interplexiform cells
Overall composition: 8-12 rows of closely packed nuclei (Fig 14.30), traversed by retinal capillaries and small arterioles (BV in Figs 14.30 and 14.34)
content.blood_supply: Unlike the outer layers of the sensory retina, the inner nuclear layer contains blood vessels: a capillary lies within the layer in the survey electron micrograph of the posterior retina, and a small arteriole is present within the inner nuclear layer (BV in Figs 14.30 and 14.34), belonging to the intraretinal microvasculature that also supplies the adjacent plexiform layers.
content.venous_drainage: The capillary blood of the inner nuclear layer, one of the vascularized strata of the sensory retina (a capillary and a small arteriole lie within the layer; BV in Figs 14.30 and 14.34), returns through the retinal veins into the central retinal vein, the vein of the retina. The central vein of the retina leaves the optic sheath anterior to the central retinal artery and joins a network of venules from the sheath, the ophthalmic artery and the adipose tissue; it drains usually into the superior ophthalmic vein, occasionally into the inferior ophthalmic vein and rarely into the cavernous sinus (Whitnall, 1932; Henry, 1959). The ophthalmic veins and their tributaries have no valves, are tortuous and end in the cavernous sinus.
content.histology_summary: HORIZONTAL CELLS serve to modulate and transform visual information received from the photoreceptors; unlike bipolar cells, whose information is relayed radially through the retina, horizontal cells form a network of fibres that integrates the activity of the photoreceptor cells horizontally. Their concentration is highest at the fovea and their number decreases towards the periphery, but their processes branch extensively as one proceeds from the central retina towards the ora serrata. Light microscopy shows short processes that radiate symmetrically from the perikaryon and long processes that stem from the base of a short process or directly from the perikaryon; the long neurite does not branch within 200-300 um of the parent horizontal cell and may reach up to 1 mm in length. Depending on the size of the cell and the extent and type of the synapses made by the dendrites and axons, three types are identified (Fig 14.31): the HI cell has long, stout dendrites that contact only cones at the triad, as well as a single axon up to 2 mm long terminating in elaborate arborizations that make one or two small punctate synapses within the invagination of the rod spherule (Kolb, 1991; Linberg and Fisher, 1992; Kolb et al., 1994); before these processes enter the invagination the axon also makes distinct synapses onto the dendrites of rod bipolar cells — an arrangement that constitutes a form of feed-forward and expands the receptive field of the rod bipolar cells beyond their dendritic field. The HIII cells are 30% larger than the HI cells and contact more cones, but are otherwise similar; the HII cells have slim overlapping dendrites and a short (100-300 um) curved axon, both of which contact cones only. The HI cells contact all spectral types of cones but their communication with the short-wavelength or blue cones is minor; the HII cells have a relatively large input from blue cones and the HIII cells have no contact with these cones (Kolb et al., 1994); thus the HI cells are presumed to function as luminosity cells and the HII and HIII types as chromaticity cells (Fig 14.32). Except for the extent of their dendrites and axons, all horizontal cells have a similar morphology: the cell body is usually flattened and has a diameter of 6-8 um; the round nucleus is surrounded by a Golgi apparatus that is frequently electron-optically empty; and the cytoplasm contains smooth and rough endoplasmic reticulum, slender mitochondria and many free ribosomes, a unique finding in retinal neurons (Sigelman and Ozanics, 1982). A characteristic feature of horizontal cells is the presence of an intracytoplasmic inclusion, the Kolmer crystalloid or body (Fig 14.29a), which consists of stacks of 5-30 parallel dense tubules separated from one another by a space of 2-6 nm; each tubule is composed of 2-3 membranes arranged concentrically and decorated on the inner and outer surfaces with ribosome-like particles; although its function is unknown, it may represent a structured rough endoplasmic reticulum. BIPOLAR CELLS are the second-order neurons of the visual circuitry, and each retina contains some 35,676,000 of them (Sigelman and Ozanics, 1982). Oriented radially in the retina, their perikarya lie in the inner nuclear layer and their processes extend to the outer and inner plexiform layers. On the basis of morphology and synaptic relationships, nine main types of bipolar cells have been distinguished (Kolb, Linberg and Fisher, 1992): rod or mop (Fig 14.33); invaginating midget; flat midget; flat diffuse or brush; invaginating diffuse; ON-centre blue cone; OFF-centre blue cone; giant bistratified; and giant diffuse invaginating. The rod bipolar cells constitute 20% of the total population and are present 1 mm from the fovea; the diameter of their dendritic tree increases from the central to the peripheral retina, and in the outer plexiform layer the main dendrite divides into 2-3 secondary branches which, after passing between the cone pedicles, arborize further into a brush-like array of processes that penetrate the invaginations of the rod spherules; the axons of the rod bipolar cells pass into the inner plexiform layer to synapse with processes of the amacrine cells and with the dendrites and cell bodies of the diffuse ganglion cells. The invaginating midget cells are the smallest of the bipolar cells: their dendrites penetrate as the central tuft in the triad of the cone pedicles, and the apical dendrite of the extrafoveal midget bipolar cells divides into two parts so that it may synapse with two different cones; their axons proceed through the inner plexiform layer and form synapses with processes of amacrine cells and dendrites of the midget ganglion cells. The flat midget bipolar cells resemble the invaginating type except that their dendrites do not deeply invaginate the cone pedicles, instead only indenting them slightly and making a superficial contact; at the fovea there is a one-to-one ratio of midget bipolar cells and cones (Kolb, Linberg and Fisher, 1992). The small-field, flat diffuse and invaginating bipolar cells have many dendritic processes with a broad expanse that terminate in the pedicles of many cones; the apical dendrite arborizes in the outer plexiform layer, its branches extend horizontally and divide into very fine tufts that terminate as aggregates in shallow depressions on the pedicles, and the small-field diffuse bipolar cells are present across the entire retina, forming an extensive overlay in the perifovea (Kolb, Linberg and Fisher, 1992). Like the diffuse bipolar cells, the blue-cone bipolars innervate more than one cone pedicle: the ON-centre or BBb variety is characterized by its axon terminal arborizing in stratum 5 of the inner plexiform layer, whereas the OFF-centre or BBa type has its axon terminal ending in stratum 1 immediately under the amacrine cell bodies; the BBb bipolar occurs at 4 mm eccentricity from the foveola, and its axon terminal, with its widely ramifying varicose structure, extends over an area of 30 um — this cell also has two sturdy dendrites that converge on the same cone as well as fine branches that end either on another cone or in the neuropil of the outer plexiform layer, while the BBa bipolar is present more towards the periphery of the retina (10 mm eccentricity). The two types of giant bipolar cells are distinguished by the extent of their dendritic spread, which exceeds 50 um in the central retina and 100 um at the periphery (Kolb, Linberg and Fisher, 1992); the giant diffuse bipolar cell has a thick major dendrite that divides into three long sinuous branches and a bistratified axon which terminates in strata 1 and 4 of the inner plexiform layer, and except for the size of its dendritic field its morphology is similar to that of the flat diffuse cells. All types of bipolar cells have a similar ultrastructure (Fig 14.33): the nucleus is round or oval with one or two nucleoli; the Golgi apparatus is prominent and is located with the centrioles at the site of origin of the main dendrite; ribosomes, rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria fill the cytoplasm, and microtubules are present in the dendrites, which are 0.1-0.2 um thick at the fovea and contain a few vesicles, 20 nm diameter filaments and many long, thin mitochondria. The axon hillock is situated opposite the origin of the dendrite, and adjacent to the cell membrane of both the dendrite and the axon are small, regularly arranged, helical tubules — structures usually found more frequently in rod bipolar cells than in other types of bipolar cells, which also contain numerous mitochondria and neurofibrils located centrally within the cell (Sigelman and Ozanics, 1982). The axons of bipolar cells contain 12.5 nm diameter neurotubules, vesicles that resemble dilated neurotubules and sparse mitochondria (Fig 14.33); up to the inner plexiform layer the axon is surrounded by processes of the Muller cells, and after shedding this glial coat the axon makes a sudden transition into the telodendrion. The telodendrion of bipolar cells has characteristic boutons which contain numerous large and complex mitochondria (Sigelman and Ozanics, 1982); synaptic vesicles are present throughout the cytoplasm in this region but are also concentrated around the synaptic ribbon; the afferent or postsynaptic processes have conventional synapses, whereas the efferent processes, which are presynaptic to amacrine or ganglion cells, have typical ribbon synapses. Most of the midget and diffuse bipolar cells (but not the rod bipolar cells) are glutamatergic; in addition, a subpopulation of bipolar perikarya (18%) and terminals (32%) exhibit strong immunolabelling for glycine (Crooks and Kolb, 1992; Davanger, Storm-Mathisen and Ottersen, 1994); the glutamate/glycine-positive terminals establish contact with amacrine cell processes and ganglion cell dendrites and are located to between 44% and 88% of the depth of the inner plexiform layer, and these cells are believed to correspond to the ON-cone/bipolar system (Davanger, Storm-Mathisen and Ottersen, 1994). MULLER CELLS occupy most of the inner intermediate layer, although their perikarya can be present in any sublayer (Fig 14.34); the mean density of Muller cells is 8-13,000 cells/mm2 (Dreher, Robinson and Distler, 1992). Embryonically, Muller cells are derived from the inner layer of the optic vesicle; during development of the retina they have an important role in the orientation, displacement and positioning of the developing neurons, and as the principal glial cells of the retina they conserve the structural alignment of its neuronal elements. Muller cells are the largest of all cells in the retina and extend from the external to the internal limiting membranes; their shape is similar to that of columnar epithelial cells, and they are characterized by their cytoplasmic expansions, which fill all intercellular spaces and envelop the cell bodies of the neurons. Four types of Muller cell processes are distinguishable (Sigelman and Ozanics, 1982): radial processes that extend from both sides of the Muller cell body in the inner plexiform layer; fine horizontal processes that extend laterally in both of the plexiform layers as well as in the nerve fibre layer; thin, villus-like projections that form the fibre baskets of Schultze around the inner segment of the photoreceptors (see p. 471); and processes that form a honeycomb meshwork which envelops the perikarya of the ganglion cells and the cells of the inner plexiform layer. Except at the external limiting membrane, where zonulae adherentes are found, tight junctions exist between Muller cells and other neuronal cells. The cytoplasm of the Muller cells shows regional morphological differences that reflect variations in the metabolic activity of these cells (Sigelman and Ozanics, 1982): the inner half of the cell contains rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a Golgi apparatus, slender mitochondria, free ribosomes and filaments 10-20 nm in diameter that are oriented radially, and its moderately electron-dense cytoplasm suggests the function of protein synthesis; the cytoplasm around the nucleus contains ribosomes and an extensive smooth endoplasmic reticulum; the outer or scleral half of the cell appears to be adapted to absorption and intracellular transport — numerous microtubules are present, mitochondria are concentrated in the cytoplasm close to the external limiting membrane, presumably providing the energy required for active transport across the outer plasma membrane, and the outer region also contains a large amount of glycogen, although this varies with the degree of oxygenation of the retina. Muller cells have an important role in the metabolism of the retina: immunohistochemical studies have revealed the presence of cellular retinaldehyde-binding proteins, glutamine, taurine and glutamine synthetase in their cytoplasm (Lewis et al., 1988; Milam et al., 1990; Pow, Crook and Wong, 1994); hybridization in situ has revealed the mRNA for carbonic anhydrase II (Rogers and Hunt, 1987; Herbert, Cavallo and Martone, 1991), which is suggested to help buffer variations in extracellular CO2 in the retina (Newman, 1994); as revealed by hybridization in situ, Muller cells cultured from rat retina contain the mRNA for insulin, which may function in the control of glucose metabolism (Das, Pansky and Bud, 1987); Muller cells are also known to degrade neurotransmitter substances (e.g. gamma-aminobutyric acid, GABA). The membrane potential across the Muller cell indicates that it has a role as a K+ electrode: the available evidence suggests that K+ ions liberated through the activity of the retinal neurons (mostly the bipolar cells) are taken up and discharged at the endfoot surface of the Muller cells into the vitreous and, in at least some species with vascularized retinas, into the retinal capillaries — in this way they contribute to the b-wave of the electroretinogram (Newman and Odette, 1984; Newman, 1987; Wen and Oakley, 1990). Experimental studies in the salamander retina have shown that activation of glutamate uptake leads to accumulation of K+ outside the Muller cells, and suppression of glutamate release from the photoreceptors by light is suggested to reduce the efflux of K+ from the Muller cells, which contributes to the light-evoked fall of K+ in the outer retina (Amato et al., 1994). AMACRINE CELLS have somas that lie internal to the nuclei of the Muller cells (Figs 14.30 and 14.34); each amacrine cell has a single process that branches extensively, has characteristics in common with both axons and dendrites, and extends over a wide area in the inner plexiform layer. The cell body of the amacrine cells has a flask or urn shape with a diameter of 12 um and, except in the fovea where they are absent, is located in the inner nuclear layer; the nucleus is round with prominent infoldings in the membrane which give it a lobulated appearance, and the abundant cytoplasm, located on the inner side of the nucleus, contains numerous mitochondria, granular endoplasmic reticulum (Nissl substance) and many electron-dense, round bodies that are probably lipoidal; a cilium is present on the inner side of the cell close to the nucleus (Sigelman and Ozanics, 1982). Amacrine cells have a diverse morphology — up to 24 varieties have been described in the human retina (Kolb, Linberg and Fisher, 1992); on the basis of the Golgi impregnation technique, two major types are distinguishable: (1) diffuse and (2) stratified. The main process of the diffuse cell type extends through the inner plexiform layer and, on the inner side of this region, arborizes to give a dense horizontal plexus; depending on the extent of these processes, the diffuse amacrine cells are further subdivided into narrow-field cells, which cover an area 10-50 um wide (average 25 um), and wide-field cells, which spread 30-50 um in the inner plexiform layer and up to 600 um in the ganglion cell layer; the wide-field diffuse amacrines make contact with rod bipolar terminals and ganglion cells. Depending on the layer in which the processes lie, the stratified amacrine cells are also further classified as unistratified, multistratified and diffuse or polystratified: the unistratified amacrine cells are located in the outer half of the inner plexiform layer, where their processes radiate horizontally for up to 500 um; the main process of the multistratified cells extends from the cell body and divides into branches that spread horizontally for 400-600 um at two or more levels, usually in the central region of the inner plexiform layer and near the ganglion cell layer; the stratified diffuse cells have smaller nuclei than the other amacrine cells and their processes cover a field of only 50 um width. Amacrine cells are also classified according to the neurotransmitter that they produce; however, no correspondence exists between this physiological classification and the morphological description. The transmitter substances associated with amacrine cell function include both neuroactive substances (acetylcholine, GABA, glycine, dopamine, serotonin) and neuropeptides (cholecystokinin, enkephalin, glucagon, neurotensin, somatostatin, substance P, neuropeptide Y and vasoactive intestinal peptide); two or more of these neuromodulating chemicals may be present in one cell, and most amacrine cells contain gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine, which have an inhibitory action on the ganglion cells (Crooks and Kolb, 1992; Davanger, Ottersen and Storm-Mathisen, 1991). INTERPLEXIFORM CELLS have nuclei that occupy the innermost part of the inner nuclear layer; because the perikarya of these cells are located among those of amacrine cells, some authors do not regard them as a separate class of cells; however, their processes extend to both plexiform layers (Kolb, Linberg and Fisher, 1992). The processes to the outer plexiform layer may arise directly from the cell body or from an interplexiform cell process in the inner plexiform layer (Fig 14.35). Sensory input to the interplexiform cell occurs in the inner plexiform layer, and most synapses are in the outer plexiform layer; thus information is carried between the two plexiform layers and the neurons appear to be centrifugal in nature. In the human retina interplexiform cells synapse onto cone horizontal cells and receive input mainly from amacrine cell processes (Linberg and Fisher, 1986); some interplexiform cells are dopaminergic. Developmentally (Wolff, Ch. 17), the inner nuclear layer is assembled from cells that migrate inward from the outer neuroblastic region. Amacrine cells — large pale round nuclei — are first seen scattered at the inner border of the outer neuroblastic layer by week 14 (embryo ~70 mm). The bipolar cells do not differentiate in the inner nuclear layer until week 23, their elongating dendrites reaching the outer plexiform layer by week 25, with the horizontal cells developing at about the same time (Rhodes, 1979). In the developed fetal layer roughly half of the somas can be positively identified as Müller cells and amacrine cells — accounting for about 35% and 11% of the total cell number respectively — with an occasional ganglion cell (1%) and the remainder probably bipolar cells (van Driel, Provis and Billson, 1990). The Müller cell nuclei at this stage are oval (on average 4.4 × 15.2 μm), often indented, and occupy the mid and vitreal regions of the layer; their darkly staining, glycogen-rich processes are already organised in a tree-like arrangement. In foveal development the layer is progressively thinned by lateral displacement — reduced to four or five rows at the fovea centre by 24-26 weeks and to fewer than three cells in the foveola by 8 months (Hendrickson and Yuodelis, 1984, 1986).
content.clinical_importance: The inner nuclear layer contains the interneurons on which all retinal signal processing depends, and its glial scaffold has direct functional correlates. The Muller cells, as the principal glia of the retina, conserve the structural alignment of the neuronal elements, guide the orientation, displacement and positioning of developing neurons, and dominate retinal metabolism: they contain cellular retinaldehyde-binding proteins, glutamine, taurine and glutamine synthetase, they carry the mRNA for carbonic anhydrase II, which helps buffer variations in extracellular CO2, they degrade neurotransmitters such as GABA, and their K+ spatial buffering — uptake of potassium liberated by neuronal activity and its discharge at the endfoot into the vitreous or the retinal capillaries — contributes to the b-wave of the electroretinogram, so Muller cell function is directly reflected in this clinical electrophysiological signal (Newman and Odette, 1984; Newman, 1987; Wen and Oakley, 1990; Amato et al., 1994). The bipolar cells carry the photoreceptor output to the inner retina: their glutamatergic midget and diffuse populations (but not the rod bipolars) and the glycine-positive subpopulation (18% of perikarya and 32% of terminals, located between 44% and 88% of the depth of the inner plexiform layer and believed to correspond to the ON-cone/bipolar system) define the chemical coding of the second-order neuron layer (Crooks and Kolb, 1992; Davanger, Storm-Mathisen and Ottersen, 1994). The amacrine cells, most of which contain inhibitory GABA and glycine acting on the ganglion cells, provide the lateral and feedback interactions that shape retinal processing, and the dopaminergic interplexiform cells link the two plexiform layers in a centrifugal direction (Linberg and Fisher, 1986; Crooks and Kolb, 1992). The absence of amacrine cells from the fovea and the high foveal concentration of horizontal cells fit the private-line midget pathways of the foveal region, and the presence of capillaries and small arterioles within the layer (Figs 14.30 and 14.34) makes it one of the vascularized strata of the sensory retina.
